title: Private deployments: VPC & On-prem deployment reference, Day-2 ops, upgrade and rollback procedures
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This document is the canonical reference for Private Deployments at Redwood Inference: VPC-based and on-prem installations, recommended reference architectures, packaging guidance, Day-2 (operational) playbooks, and prescriptive upgrade and rollback procedures. It consolidates customer requirements and provides checklists, SLOs, and concrete CLI/YAML examples to be used by solutions engineers, SREs, and customer ops teams.

Scope
- Target audience: Solutions Engineering, Customer Engineering, SRE, Field Ops, and Enterprise customers deploying Redwood Private.
- Included: VPC deployments, air-gapped / on-prem packaging, day-2 operations, deterministic upgrade and rollback procedures, and a customer requirements library.
- Excluded: Hosted API onboarding (see product-docs) and model training guidance.

Goals
- Provide a single, reproducible playbook for deploying and operating Redwood Private.
- Reduce time-to-first-request for customers by providing validated templates and runbooks.
- Ensure upgrades follow safe, observable steps with clear rollback paths.

Ownership and SLA
- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments team (oncall: private-deployments@redwood.ai).
- Secondary: eng-sre for infra and capacity questions.
- Operational SLA (customer-facing): 99.5% availability for control-plane APIs and 99.0% for inference endpoints (for Dedicated/Private when SLA contract is in place). Internal readiness checks run at 1-minute intervals.

Prerequisites and customer requirements
Provide this checklist to customers before starting a deployment. Each item below maps to a section in the customer requirements library.

1) Network and connectivity
- VPC CIDR ranges (primary and peered): 10.10.0.0/16 (example).
- NAT / egress policy: Support for TLS egress to Redwood package repositories (or allow offline packaging).
- Allowed ports (control-plane and data-plane): 443 (control), 10250-10255 (k8s node ports), 9000-9100 (inference runtime ports).
- Private peering requirements (if using cross-account peering): account IDs and route table updates.

2) Identity and secrets
- KMS or HSM for key management (AWS KMS, Azure KeyVault, or on-prem HSM).
- Service account and RBAC mappings for control-plane components.

3) Compute and storage
- Minimum GPU node profile: 2x A10G or equivalent per replica for production inference.
- Storage: 1 TB NVMe per node recommended for model cache.
- Persistent volumes: CSI-compatible NFS/CEPH/CloudBlock.

4) Observability and logging
- Syslog / Fluentd endpoint or object storage bucket for centralized logs.
- Prometheus scrape targets and retention policy (see Observability section).

Reference architectures (summaries)
Below are 3 validated reference architectures. Choose based on customer constraints (latency, data residency, air-gapped).

1) VPC-managed (cloud) - Recommended for most enterprise customers
- Control plane in customer VPC (private subnets) with optional peering to Redwood control plane for telemetry.
- Dedicated GPU pool in private subnets behind an NLB.
- Autoscaling group managed via infra tooling with node pool draining hooks.

2) Hybrid (control plane in Redwood, runtime in customer VPC)
- Control plane runs in Redwood-managed tenancy; runtime (inference) runs in customer VPC behind private link.
- Suitable when customers cannot host management plane but require data-residency for inference.

3) On-prem / Air-gapped
- Full control plane and runtime packaged for private registry / offline installation.
- Uses local KMS/HSM and internal image registry.
- Requires manual cadence for image/package updates.

VPC Deployment guide (step-by-step)
High-level phases: Preparation -> Provisioning -> Validation -> Handover.

Preparation
- Confirm CIDR, peering, and firewall rules using the Customer Requirements checklist.
- Exchange SSH keys and service account metadata.
- Validate access to package repo or confirm offline package delivery.

Provisioning (example using Terraform + Helm)
1. Bootstrap infra: create VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT, and security groups.
2. Provision EKS/GKE/AKS cluster with recommended node pool labels: role=private-inference, gpu=true.
3. Apply storage classes and CSI drivers.
4. Install Redwood control-plane components via Helm:

Commands (example):
- terraform apply -var=cluster_name=redwood-private-cluster
- kubectl create namespace redwood-control-plane
- helm repo add redwood https://packages.redwood.ai/helm
- helm upgrade --install redwood-control redwood/redwood-control --namespace redwood-control-plane -f values-production.yaml

Validation (smoke tests)
- Check pods: kubectl -n redwood-control-plane get pods -o wide (expect all pods Running)
- Health endpoints: curl -sS https://redwood-control.internal/healthz
- API request: curl -X POST \"https://redwood-control.internal/v1/deployments/health-check\" -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'

On-prem packaging and installation notes
- Packaging: We provide an air-gapped bundle (tar.gz) with Helm charts, images (OCI layout), and a manifest.json signed by Redwood.
- Installation steps: import OCI images to local registry, apply manifests with kubeadm/helm, configure KMS endpoint to local HSM.
- Deterministic manifests: manifests are tagged with SHA and release tag (e.g., redwood-release-2026-02-01-sha256:abcdef).

Day-2 operations (runbooks)
Common operational actions and runbook references. Each runbook below is a numbered procedure.

A) Scaling inference capacity
1. Evaluate current utilization: prometheus query (rate: requests per second, GPU utilization).
2. If utilization > 70% sustained (15m), increase node pool by N nodes: terraform apply -var=worker_count=+2.
3. Monitor rollout and check model latency SLO (95th percentile).

B) Evacuate node for maintenance
1. cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>
2. drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
3. Replace instance and uncordon after health checks.

C) Rotating certificates / keys
1. Start rotation window during low traffic.
2. Generate new certs in KMS, update secrets in k8s (kubectl apply -f rotated-secrets.yaml).
3. Restart control-plane pods with rolling restart: kubectl rollout restart deploy -n redwood-control-plane
4. Verify connectivity and metrics.

Upgrade and rollback procedures (recommended, production)
Principles:
- Always run upgrades in a canary -> staged -> full rollout sequence.
- Back up state: etcd snapshot, model cache metadata, and control-plane DB before major upgrades.
- Maintain immutable release artifacts (tagged images and Helm charts).

Upgrade steps (minor patch):
1. Pre-checks: verify cluster health, SLO windows, and run smoke tests.
2. Canary: deploy new release to a single replica or canary node pool (label: rollout=canary).
3. Observe for 30 minutes (monitor errors, p95 latency, token cost).
4. If green, promote to staged (25% of capacity) for 60 minutes.
5. Full rollout: upgrade remaining replicas via Helm with maxUnavailable set to safe value.

Commands (example):
- helm upgrade redwood-control redwood/redwood-control -f values-2026-02-canary.yaml --namespace redwood-control-plane
- kubectl set image deploy/redwood-runtime redwood-runtime=redwood/runtime:2026-02-01-shaabcdef

Rollback steps (if canary or staged shows regression)
1. Immediate action: scale down canary replicas and route traffic back to previous release.
2. helm rollback redwood-control <previous_revision> --namespace redwood-control-plane
3. Restore state if data migrations were part of the failed release (use etcd snapshot restore instructions).
4. Postmortem: tag release as failed and create a regression issue with failing metrics/samples.

Emergency rollback (fast path)
- If inference latency or error rate exceeds critical thresholds (error rate > 5% or p95 latency > 2x baseline), trigger emergency rollback: set routing policy to fallback model variant and rollback Helm release to previous stable revision.

Testing and validation for upgrades
- Canary tests: synthetic prompts covering top-10 customer prompt shapes.
- Monitoring: prometheus rules for increase in 5xx errors, p95 latency, and GPU OOM signals.
- Automated rollback policy: if 5xx_rate > 0.5% for 5m, rollback automatically.

Customer requirements library (condensed)
Provide this trimmed library to customer pre-engagement. Each requirement is tagged in the internal ticketing system for check-off.

- Network: outbound TLS to packages.redwood.ai OR offline bundle acceptance.
- Storage: support for CSI driver listed in our compatibility matrix.
- Monitoring: Prometheus endpoint reachable by our observability agents (or a push gateway).
- Secrets: KMS integration (supported providers: AWS KMS 1.0+, Azure KeyVault, HashiCorp Vault 1.8+).
- Compliance: SOC2/ISO mapping document and required audit log retention (default 365 days).

Operational runbook snippets and snippets for common issues
- Recovering a stuck model worker: kill pod, check model cache corruption logs (/var/log/redwood/model-cache.log), rehydrate from central model store.
- Clearing KV cache safely: curl -X POST https://redwood-control.internal/v1/cache/clear -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '{"model":"<model-name>","prefix":"<prefix>"}'

Appendix: example values-production.yaml (truncated)
| component | recommended | notes |
|---|---|---|
| replicaCount | \"3\" | control-plane replicas; adjust by SLA |
| nodePool.gpu | \"true\" | node selector label for GPU nodes |
| storage.cacheSize | \"100Gi\" | per-node model cache recommended size |

values-production.yaml (example snippet):
---
replicaCount: 3
nodePool:
  gpu: true
  instanceType: a10g.large
storage:
  cacheSize: 100Gi
  className: gp2
